catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-1-q2.explanation: forerunner A forerunner is a person or thing that comes first, and then something else follows. Also known as precursor. Pioneer here isn’t good enough because it doesn’t imply that something else came after it. Moreover, it is normally used to refer to people rather than things.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-1-q3.explanation: D - inspired To inspire is to make someone do something by positive means. For example a writer needs inspiration to produce a good work. This inspiration can be anything — a friend, a place he likes, his favourite food or drink. Other suggested variants do not fit here either because of meaning or context.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-1-q4.explanation: A - breakthroughIt means that some great progress was achieved or a serious obstacle overcome successfully. Leap and step aren’t strong enough to convey the meaning of what is talked about in the second part of the sentence. Headway implies gradual progress rather than sudden one.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-1-q5.explanation: C - stoodTo stand somebody in good stead means to become useful at some point. In this case his experience of organizing an even became useful later. Other verbs do not collocate with stead here.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-1-q6.explanation: C - aloneLet alone means much less, not no mention. It means here than not many people have been to Egypt and even fewer had the chance to travel the route that Mr. Cook was using for his tours.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-1-q7.explanation: B - goingTo go back when used with time means the age of it, in this case the Egyptian civilisation. Other phrasal verbs here do not collocate with context.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-1-q8.explanation: D - world ‘The world of …’ phrase means some area of interest, industry etc., for example The new collection by Armani changed the world of fashion, The world of chemistry was surprised by this year’s Nobel Prize winner. Other words do not fit as ‘The world of …’ is a set expression.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-2-q9.explanation: A proposal or offer is usually followed by the preposition ‘for’ or the ‘to do’ infinitive. We can only use the first one because of context limitations.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-2-q10.explanation: suchFor such a machine here means for a machine like this one.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-2-q11.explanation: To consist of something is used to say what something is made up of or contains. Prospective buyers for such a machine would be laboratories and government institutions. Prospective buyers for such a machine would be laboratories and government institutions.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-2-q12.explanation: Remember the text is in the past tense, so the verb ‘to be’ must be in its past form: ‘were’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-2-q13.explanation: toTo be here refers to the future sales. Will be is incorrect because it would need that placed before the verb.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-2-q14.explanation: otherCant use another here because artefacts is in plural. An artefact is an object made by a human being, typically one of cultural or historical interest.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-2-q16.explanation: These/Those/TheyAll of these words are possible. We know we have to use the plural form because of the previous sentence and the auxiliary verb.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-3-q17.explanation: phenomenalThe only difficulty here is spelling the word correctly. It is evident from context that you need to use an adjective in this case.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-3-q18.explanation: centralSame as the previous word, mind the spelling.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-3-q19.explanation: Lasting means ‘taking place for a long time’. ‘Latest’ is incorrect — it would imply that the film got its acclaim recently, but in truth it has always been popular.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-3-q20.explanation: To be unsuited to something means to lack the necessary qualities or temperament for it, which fits the context of her rejecting that life. ‘Unsuitable’ is wrong as it implies that Rhett isn’t appropriate to the Hollywood star life, she isn’t fit for it. This isn’t implied by context.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-3-q21.explanation: contemporariesA contemporary is a person that lived in the same period of time, but not necessarily of the same age.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-3-q22.explanation: producersKeep in mind that the word has to be pluralised because it is used in conjunction with plural ‘agents’. If the word had to be in singular, it would need a definite or indefinite article.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-3-q23.explanation: signedDon’t confuse ‘photograph’ and ‘autograph’. The second word would require a different word — ‘signing’. A signed autograph is an autograph with the person’s signature on it.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-3-q24.explanation: unansweredWithout an answer. Make sure you use the right negative prefix.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-4-q25.answer: haven’t/have not got round to answering
catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-4-q25.explanation: haven’t/have not got round to answering‘Get round to doing something’ means to find time or opportunity to do it. Don’t forget to use gerund form.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-4-q26.explanation: ‘Matter of minutes/hours/years’ etc. says how much time said activity took place; it can be used to denote how much (or little) time some aciton, even or activity takes to happen.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-4-q27.explanation: no doubt (that) things will get‘Bound to’ means ‘very likely to’. If there is no doubt about something, then the speaker is sure of it.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-4-q28.answer: was Jake who/that got me interested
catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-4-q28.explanation: was Jake who/that got me interestedKeep in mind that in the paper-based test all of your Use of English letters have to be capitalised.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-4-q29.explanation: was desperate to give‘To be desperate to do something’ means that the person has strong desire to do it.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-4-q30.explanation: injury prevented him from playing‘To prevent’ means to stop something from happening. Mind the preposition (‘from’) and the gerund form.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-5-q31.explanation: COne of the meanings of project is that it requires considerable effort and preparation. The following sentences describe how seriously and thoroughly Chanu prepared for his sightseeing tour. Answer A isn’t mentioned — there is nothing about a sense of duty in the text. Answer B is wrong as the first sentence clearly states that he decided to go sightseeing only after having spent 30 years in London. Answer D isn’t correct — even though Chanu made serious preparations for it, it isn’t stated that these preparations were necessary.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-5-q32.explanation: CThe phrases used to describe his appearance are clearly used for humorous effect (shorts hanging mid-calf is clearly an exaggeration).

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-5-q33.explanation: ALast sentence of the second paragraph contains the answer. ‘barely had time to lift my head’ means that he didn’t have time to go see the sights before. He regrets this fact at the beginning of the paragraph, saying that he ‘hardly left these streets’. Other answers mention insignificant details or aren’t mentioned at all (like answer B).

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-5-q34.explanation: DParagraph 4 and the beginning of Paragraph 5 have the answer. When Chanu asks them about their mood, he gets mixed responses: Bibi enjoys it, Shahana seems to be bored and Chanu himself hums a melody because of his high spirits. Answer A is wrong — nothing is said about Nazneen’s attitude to the amount of food. Answer B is not correct as Shahana clearly shows her discontent, therefore she doesn’t pretend to enjoy it. Answer C is incorrect — Chanu explained why he himself came, and nothing is said about why he brought the family along.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-5-q35.explanation: BParagraph starting with ‘The conductor ….’. At the end of the paragraph-sentence, the conductor was considering whether to make Chanu get off the bus — he was trying to understand if he was a possible troublemaker. Answers A and C are not mentioned. Answer D relates to conductor’s question about Chanu’s home country — he asked that not because he misunderstood him, but to give better guidance.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-5-q36.explanation: BAs it was mentioned at the very beginning of this text, Chanu has spent over 30 years living in London, so the term ‘local’ (person that has been living there since birth or for a very long time) could be used to describe Chanu as well.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-6-q37.explanation: BSentence three says that he was too gullible (believing everything he gets said too easily, without scepticism.) and the ‘questionable advice of key figures around him’ could be blamed for the damage that his policies caused. Other reviewers believe that he should be blamed personally.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-6-q38.explanation: AReviewer A speaks of policies that he personally championed against considerable opposition’ — meaning that many people were against these decisions. Speaker D concurs: the politician ‘carried on regardless of the inadvisability of doing so’ — people advised against continuing his policy, but he chose to do it his way.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-6-q39.explanation: ASpeaker A is the only one who believes that the politician pursued his personal interests (second part of sentence one). Others hold the view that his prime motivation was to serve his own country.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-6-q40.explanation: DBoth A and D believe that the greatest feat was narrowing the gap between the poor and the rich. Speaker A mentions it in the second part of their paragraph and Speaker Dsays that at the very end: ‘he made society more equal’ and then clarifying that many ‘not so well-off’ (poor) members of that society really benefited from his policies.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-7-q41.explanation: FParagraph F continues the theme of the introduction and ends by mentioning a study dedicated to the therapeutic effects of singing in choirs. The next paragraph starts with ‘there was a specific angle to this study‘. Even though there are some paragraphs with fitting beginnings, their endings do not fit the following paragraph.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-7-q42.explanation: B‘I take no issue’ and ‘I take no argument’ are followed one by another for emphatic (stronger) effect. At the end of Paragraph B the author complains how this information about singing is never put to good use, and the next paragraph states that there are occasional attempts to do so. Paragraph C fits well here, but it’s ending is much better used later on.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-7-q43.explanation: GThe idea of schools not willing to host such events is expanded in this and the previous paragraph. At the end of Paragraph G a ‘worthwhile singing project’ is mentioned —this is the project that starts the next paragraph — ‘Noye’s Fludde’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-7-q44.explanation: CThe ending of Paragraph C and the beginning of next paragraph talk about the author’s one-time experience of singing in choir.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-7-q45.explanation: EThe main topic of this and the previous paragraph is access to ‘that world’ — the world of music, the world of possibilities. The health benefits are only a ‘bonus’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-7-q46.explanation: AThis paragraph is the only one where Britten is mentioned. The singing sessions, mentioned in the paragraph above, are told here to be ‘extraordinary experience’ for all the children that participated.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-8-q47.explanation: C Last sentence of the text. The tower had been closed and demolished (destroyed)

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-8-q48.explanation: ASecond sentence of paragraph two says that the artist ‘does not seek to confirm how the world looks’. This means that the works are fairly abstract rather than objective in their nature.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-8-q49.explanation: CFirst sentence of the paragraph mentions that most find the industrial sites ‘unsightly’ — not very pretty or outright ugly.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-8-q50.explanation: BIn the middle of second paragraph the author describes his own interpretation of his picture, which is rather different from other people’s.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-8-q51.explanation: BSecond paragraph, second half of it, tells of how the artist had to put the painting in bathtub to achieve certain colour or artistic effect.Next sentence says that it can be dangerous because the results can’t be controlled.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-8-q52.explanation: DIn the lower part of the second paragraph, the artist mentions how he comes to the same cafe twice to make sure that no minor details are missing from his painting.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-8-q53.explanation: BThe last sentence of second paragraph mentions how the artist reworked everything to ‘establish links throughout the composition’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-8-q54.explanation: BThe very first sentence says that he uses both studio and open-air locations for painting. We can’t use Paragraph A for the answer even though the artist mentions exploring the coastline. This is because the question is asked in Present Simple, meaning that the artist does that on a regular basis. Paragraph A talks of an experience that is in the past.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-8-q55.explanation: AThe artist states that the painting is ‘the largest I’ve ever attempted’. It is the size of the painting that makes it different from other works of the same author.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test4-part-8-q56.explanation: DThe author looks for ‘bespoke interiors’ and individuals that attend those pubs.
